claims.text: Applying a Si-20Cr-20Fe silicide coating to MoNbTaTiW will improve its high-temperature oxygen resistance.
The substrate is an equimolar MoNbTaTiW refractory high-entropy alloy.
The MoNbTaTiW substrate can be produced by spark plasma sintering or arc melting.
The initial MoNbTaTiW alloy has a continuous BCC solid-solution microstructure.
A Si-20Cr-20Fe coating can be deposited on MoNbTaTiW by a fused-slurry method and heat-treated at 1430 °C for 1 hour under vacuum.
The specified heat treatment produces a well-bonded, uniform coating.
The coated alloy is intended to resist oxidation in static air at temperatures from 1000 to 1300 °C for approximately 1 hour.
The initial coating contains high-silicon MSi2 and lower-silicon M5Si3 silicide layers.
High-temperature oxidation transforms the silicide coating into a surface oxide layer.
The resulting oxide scale is adherent and dense.
The oxide scale comprises SiO2, chromium-containing oxides such as CrTaO4, and TiO2.
Silicon and chromium from the coating diffuse into the MoNbTaTiW substrate surface during high-temperature exposure.
Oxidation of the coating-derived silicide phases yields a protective oxide layer.
The dense oxide scale suppresses oxygen diffusion into the alloy and thereby lowers the oxidation rate.
Uncoated MoNbTaTiW forms thick, porous, rapidly growing oxide scales with high weight gain during high-temperature air exposure.
Relative to uncoated MoNbTaTiW, coated samples will have lower weight gain and a thinner oxide scale after 1 hour at 1000–1300 °C.
The predicted benefit is limited to short-duration static-air exposure, while long-term cyclic behavior remains uncertain.
The magnitude of the oxidation-rate and scale-thickness reductions is unknown and may depend on coating uniformity and processing details.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in both weight gain and oxide-scale thickness relative to an identically exposed uncoated control would falsify the hypothesis.
